summary: Deep technical session focusing on p95/p99 tail causes for streaming vs non-streaming paths. Walkthrough of Redwood runtime adaptive stream->nonstream fallback, KV cache hotkeys, batching/window sizing, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem network hop impacts. Agreed next steps for profiling run and shared artifacts.
topics: KV cache hotkeys and shard affinity
batching window sizing and tokenization impact
transcript:
[00:00] Jamal Ortega: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Lena Park: Lena here, hi.
[00:08] Marcus Zhou: Marcus, SRE.
[00:10] Anita Rao: Anita, ML lead.
[00:12] Priya Desai: Priya from Redwood, hi all.
[00:15] Marco Li: Marco joining.
[00:17] Jamal Ortega: Cool. So goal for today is a deep dive on tail behavior we're seeing — p95/p99 spikes — and walk through the adaptive stream fallback we mentioned. We'll try to map symptoms to root causes and agree next steps.
[01:02] Lena Park: The big issue for us is intermittent p99 blips that happen during bursts, mostly when our front-end enables long-streaming sessions. They look like 800ms to 1.4s spikes even though median is fine.
[01:28] Marcus Zhou: Right, and most of those correlate with a specific set of prompts that are long and include multimodal tokens — tokenization varies. We captured traces.
[01:42] Priya Desai: Thanks — those traces were super helpful. Before we jump in, quick note: our "adaptive stream fallback" is the pattern where the runtime starts streaming output but, under resource/latency pressure, falls back to a non-streaming, batched path to preserve throughput. We use that for tight latency SLOs to avoid head-of-line blocking.
[02:20] Anita Rao: Wait — can you clarify: when you say "fall back to non-streaming" do you mean you buffer the whole decode and then return at once? That seems like it would increase tail if not done carefully.
[02:34] Priya Desai: Good callout. There are two variants: a) partial-streaming where we keep sending prefix tokens and then batch remaining tokens to finish, and b) full fallback where we stop streaming and finish in a batched non-stream pipeline. The latter can increase p95 if there's extra serialization/IO, but it avoids repeated tiny kernel launches that blow up cost.
[03:10] Marcus Zhou: Our ops team noticed increased network hops in those windows; requests cross an edge proxy to a VPC egress and then to a private cluster. The extra RTTs amplify the tail.
[03:33] Jamal Ortega: Classic amplification: small increases in per-hop latency become visible at p99. We often see the streaming path sensitive to multi-hop jitter because it does many small writes.
[04:05] Marco Li: Quick interruption — one observation from our benchmarks: streaming gives lower median but higher variance with small writes; non-streamed batched calls have higher median single-request but tighter tail. So trade-off depends on request size distribution.
[04:30] Priya Desai: Exactly. That's why we recommend adaptive policies: prefer streaming for short-turn prompts, prefer non-stream for long-turn or high-concurrency workloads, and a hybrid partial-stream if you need graceful UX.
[05:02] Lena Park: In our case, users are sensitive to perceived responsiveness for the first tokens. If the first chunk is slow, engagement drops.
[05:15] Anita Rao: Also we have a hot KV cache for certain common prefixes, but when the hot-shard moves we see a cascade of cold misses and p99 spikes.
[05:29] Priya Desai: Hot-shard behavior is a big one. Our runtime tracks prefix K V cache hits and we do sticky routing to keep affinity. But in VPC/on-prem setups, sharding constraints + autoscaler churn can move the hot shard. That can cause temporary cold-paths with higher KV fetch latencies.
[06:05] Marcus Zhou: And our network team saw TCP retransmits during those windows — maybe due to MTU mismatch with the edge proxy.
[06:20] Jamal Ortega: Yikes. Ok, let's list probable root causes: network multi-hop jitter; KV hot-shard movement; batching/window sizing mismatch; fallback path serialization overhead; quantization and kernel slowdowns for certain sequence lengths.
[06:47] Tom Chen: And don't forget: when we enable 4-bit quantization for cost, some kernels under certain seq-lens go through a slower emulation path. We saw regression at p99 when sequence length > 1k.
[07:04] Priya Desai: Yes, quantization caveats are real. For some architectures we recommend 4-bit for throughput but fallback to int8 or fp16 for long-seq workloads. We can set model-variant routing rules to avoid bad combos.
[07:30] [07:30] Speaker 6: Sorry, quick question — how does streaming impact TCP connection patterns? Are you opening many small connections?
[07:37] Priya Desai: Good question. We typically keep connections pooled, but streaming means frequent small writes which can cause Nagle interactions and cause coalescing or delays if not tuned. For on-prem we suggest TCP_NODELAY on the edge proxies and smaller write buffer thresholds.
[08:05] Jamal Ortega: Let's walk through a sample trace — high level. (shared link) slides: https://redwood.app/decks/cypherware-adaptive-latency-walkthrough.pdf and raw traces: https://redwood.app/traces/cypherware/p99-spike-12-01.csv
[08:38] Priya Desai: Look at 00:18 in the trace — you can see multiple small write syscalls across three network hops. The application-level latency for the first chunk gets split across those hops and then they queue before the GPU decode starts.
[09:10] Marcus Zhou: That map corresponds with our ingress edge -> egress NAT -> private cluster hop pattern. We do egress NAT for auditing.
[09:25] Priya Desai: Egress NAT and audit logging add one more serialization point. For streaming, each token chunk may pass through audit pipeline which batches at a different cadence. That mismatch adds jitter.
[10:02] Anita Rao: Could prefix KV caching reduce the number of kernel launches?
[10:12] Priya Desai: Yes if you hit KV cache, we avoid re-loading the full key-value and can reuse cached KV; that reduces kernel time and improves tail. But the cache must be warmed and sharded correctly. Our runtime uses a per-shard LRU and an async prefetcher for popular prefixes — but it needs accurate popularity signals.
[10:43] Marco Li: On the batching topic: we saw that increasing the batching window from 5ms to 20ms reduces GPU idle stalls but increases median by ~30ms. However the p99 improved because more requests could be coalesced and avoid micro-launch overheads.
[11:05] Jamal Ortega: So for Cypherware's workload — mix of long prompts with some short interactive queries — we may want an adaptive batching window: small window early for first-chunk streaming, then expand window for tail tokens.
[11:28] Lena Park: That sounds promising. How invasive is that to implement?
[11:33] Priya Desai: On Redwood side it's an existing policy flag — we can enable an "early-send" + "adaptive window" profile. For on-prem we may need to tune kernel selection for quantized model variants.
[11:52] Marcus Zhou: Network-wise, we can reduce proxy hops by colocating audit function in the same VPC or by doing in-line sampling instead of full egress. We'll test that.
[12:12] Priya Desai: Great. One more nuance: streaming vs non-stream change also affects KV cache topology because streaming tends to keep the session affinity longer, while batched requests can land on different backends unless affinity is enforced. So ensure sticky session or request-level affinity for sequences.
[12:40] Anita Rao: Any guidance on quantized kernel regressions for long seqs?
[12:46] Priya Desai: We maintain a per-model profile. For sequences > 1k tokens, some 4-bit kernels switch to an emulated path that has worse latency. Our engineer notes: prefer 8-bit for long-form generation or use a mixed-precision variant that switches at runtime. We can push a model-variant rule: route long seqs to fp16 variant, short to 4-bit.
[13:20] Jamal Ortega: Let's talk instrumentation because you team needs to confirm root cause. Recommended profiling: TCP-level RTT histograms, kernel launch latency histograms, KV cache hit/miss counters per shard, and tracing that correlates request id across edge proxies and GPU worker.
[13:44] Marcus Zhou: We've got tcpdump and eBPF tracing but pairing those with application request IDs has been manual.
[13:52] Priya Desai: We'll share a small tracer snippet that injects a unique request id header and a recommended eBPF mapping. Also we'll provide an example Grafana dashboard.
[14:10] Jamal Ortega: We'll also run a 48h soak with your representative prompt set in our staging with both streaming-only, non-stream-only, and adaptive profiles. Priya will lead the kernel-level profiling.
[14:26] Marco Li: I'll note that one configuration we saw that helped: set batching max tokens to 512, early-send threshold at 32 tokens, and enable prefix-KV prefetch for top-50 prefixes. That gave good median and stable p99 on a mixed workload.
[14:50] Anita Rao: What's the risk of prefix prefetch increasing memory pressure on GPUs?
[14:56] Priya Desai: It does increase KV memory footprint. We can constrain prefetch depth and use eviction heuristics. For on-prem with limited GPU RAM, we'll pick conservative prefetch settings and measure.
[15:20] Jamie (redacted): [Crosstalk] — mention of SLOs?
[15:25] Jamal Ortega: SLOs — you mentioned target p95 200ms and p99 450ms earlier, right Anita?
[15:30] Anita Rao: Yes that's our product target.
[15:33] Priya Desai: Ok then our profile must optimize for p99 under that target. That likely means hybrid stream->partial-stream path and routing long-run to int8/fp16.
[16:00] [16:00] Lena Park: Let's dig into a concrete example. We saw a spike at 11:02am last week; the trace shows repeated small writes and then a KV miss for prefix-xyz.
[16:18] Priya Desai: If you look at the attached trace row 234, the request did 7 small writes, each 8–12ms, and there was a 120ms gap for KV fetch because cache miss triggered async load from remote store. That remote load hit a different availability zone which added 80ms network RTT. So multi-hop + cache miss stacked up.
[16:50] Marcus Zhou: So we need both better cache warming and avoidance of cross-AZ calls for those hot prefixes. We'll try pinning those shards to same AZ.
[17:05] Priya Desai: Good plan. Also consider local persistent KV store for on-prem to avoid remote fetches entirely.
[17:22] Marco Li: On the quantization front, we discovered one more weirdness: throughput optimized kernels sometimes assume a tokenization chunk size and do padding that increases compute for short prompts. That affects median but can also increase p99 when combined with network jitter.
[17:48] Anita Rao: Any immediate mitigations we can try?
[17:52] Priya Desai: Short list: 1) Enable early-send for first chunk; 2) Increase batching window slightly after first chunk to coalesce tail tokens; 3) Pin hot KV shards to AZ; 4) Adjust TCP_NODELAY and write buffer at proxies; 5) Route long sequences to int8/fp16 model variant.
[18:18] Jamal Ortega: For the on-prem flavor, additional items: ensure the edge proxy and audit pipeline are co-located, validate MTU and avoid extra NATs, and disable Nagle where appropriate.
[18:40] Marcus Zhou: We'll run network-level tests. Also, is there an easy way to see when the runtime switches variants so we can correlate p99 to variant-switches?
[18:53] Priya Desai: Yes, runtime emits a short event trace with variant id and reason for switch. We'll add that event into the request trace so you can filter by variant.
[19:06] Anita Rao: Great. One more question: how do we avoid amplification during autoscaler churn?
[19:12] Priya Desai: We recommend controlled scaling with graceful drain windows and pre-warming new nodes with popular model shards. Also prefer gradual scale-up with buffer capacity rather than instant scale to avoid hot shard relocation.
[19:30] Jamal Ortega: OK let's capture testing plan: 48h soak in staging with injected network jitter experiments (0/10/50ms), three runtime profiles (stream-only, non-stream-only, adaptive), quantization variants (4-bit, int8, fp16), and KV prefetch configs. We'll collect p50/p95/p99, per-hop RTTs, kernel launch latency histograms, and shard-level cache metrics.
[20:12] Marcus Zhou: We'll provide the staging VPC creds and sample traces.
[20:20] Priya Desai: We'll draft a profiling playbook and the exact CLI commands.
[20:28] Jamal Ortega: Any other open questions?
[20:33] Lena Park: Not yet, but can you also include a recommendation for UX fallback — if p99 exceeds threshold show a partial response with progressive enhancement?
[20:44] Priya Desai: Yeah that's a UI pattern: optimistic streaming for first tokens and then gracefully degrade to a placeholder while backend finishes. We can share best practices.
[21:00] [21:00] (discussion moves to scheduling next meeting and clarifying responsibilities)
[24:30] Jamal Ortega: Quick recap — action items we already captured. We'll share slides and CSV; Priya will run profiling and share results; Marcus provides network setup; Anita provides prompt set and SLO matrix. Follow-up on 2027-12-15.
[25:05] Lena Park: Thanks all.
[25:07] Anita Rao: Thanks.
[25:09] Priya Desai: Thanks everybody — we'll send notes.
[25:12] Jamal Ortega: Meeting adjourned.
